analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for the President or Vice President to sell or trade on confidential government information.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 3, 2026 and placed on the Senate calendar the next day; the Senate has taken no further action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a new federal crime: the President or Vice President may not sell, exchange, or monetize information learned through their official position that has not been made public. Anyone who buys such information can also be prosecuted. Penalties include up to five years in prison, fines up to double the deal's value, forfeiture of profits, and civil penalties of up to three times the gain, with liability extending to companies the official controls or largely owns. The statute of limitations pauses while the official is in office.
analysis.who_benefits: The public gets a new tool against a president or vice president monetizing confidential government information, including through family-controlled businesses, with criminal fines, forfeiture of profits, and civil penalties of up to three times the gain; enforcement is by the Justice Department, and the clock on lawsuits pauses while the official holds office.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens opposed to official self-dealing

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison and fines up to double the transaction value, for the President or Vice President to sell or exchange information gained through their office for financial benefit.

It bars anyone from buying such information, cutting off the market, and imposes civil penalties up to three times the gain plus forfeiture of profits, enforceable by the Attorney General with a six-year window that pauses while the official holds office.

It creates joint liability for companies controlled by or more than 5 percent owned by the President or Vice President, and requires the Office of Government Ethics to refer credible evidence to the Justice Department and notify the Judiciary Committees.

analysis.who_pays: A president or vice president who would otherwise be able to sell or trade on confidential government information, and anyone — including businesses they control — who would buy it, now faces prison, fines, and disgorgement of profits.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only the President and Vice President, not members of Congress, federal judges, or other senior executive officials, so it leaves most holders of nonpublic government information outside the ban.

Enforcement depends on the Attorney General (a political appointee serving at the President's pleasure) choosing to bring civil or criminal cases, and on the Office of Government Ethics referring credible evidence; a resistant administration could leave the law dormant.

Because the bill restricts information the President 'gains as a result of the covered person's official position,' critics could argue it intrudes on the President's ability to communicate, though the ban applies only to transactions made for financial benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core prohibition on monetizing confidential government information is a straightforward integrity measure with few costs; the main weaknesses are narrow coverage (two offices), reliance on the Administration's own Justice Department for enforcement, and selective scope that reads as aimed at one President rather than a comprehensive ethics overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, placed on the calendar for possible floor action, and has not been brought up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Padilla introduced the bill on August 3, 2026, with four Democratic cosponsors.
The next day it was read a second time and placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 536, where bills wait for a leader's decision to bring them up.
No committee referral, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one has gained or lost anything, since the bill has not been brought to a vote; the President and Vice President remain subject only to existing conflict-of-interest rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the bill sits untouched.

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corrupt Trading Act and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Peters, and Merkley

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans have joined, and the bill sits on a Senate calendar controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Entities and individuals who would buy or monetize presidential information
industries.note: The bill makes it illegal for anyone to purchase or trade on nonpublic government information from the President or Vice President, closing a previously unpoliced channel. Anyone relying on such access for market advantage faces criminal fines, forfeiture, and civil disgorgement.

industries.industry: Private businesses controlled by or majority-owned by the President or Vice President
industries.note: Companies controlled by, or more than 5 percent owned by, a covered official are directly liable for deals involving their information. Because the bill only covers the two top executive offices, other officials' business empires remain untouched.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship, no committee action, and no signs of Republican or leadership support, the bill will most likely sit on the Senate calendar and expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a floor vote.
